stem:
A 41-year-old man attends the emergency department with a deep thigh abscess that the registrar plans to incise and drain. The microbiology team have not yet reported any cultures and he looks well with normal observations.

On what basis should the doctor choose his personal protective equipment for this procedure?

options.A: The culture result, once the laboratory has reported it
options.B: Whether the man appears systemically unwell
options.C: What the triage nurse wore when she assessed him
options.D: The likely exposure to blood and pus during drainage
options.E: How long the procedure is likely to take

correct_answer: D. The likely exposure to blood and pus during drainage
why_correct: Under standard infection control precautions, PPE is chosen by assessing the foreseeable exposure to blood and body fluids for the specific task. Incising an abscess carries a risk of splashing, so gloves, an apron and eye or face protection are appropriate whatever the culture result or how well he looks. Source: National Infection Prevention and Control Manual for England, standard infection control precautions, NHS England, 2022 (updated online).
why_wrong: A. PPE is needed now, long before any culture result is back. B. A well-looking patient can still pose a splash and contamination risk. C. A colleague doing a different task faced a different exposure. E. Duration does not determine the risk of contact with blood and pus.
pearl: Standard precautions treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, so protection is based on the task rather than the patient's known infection status.
thinking: Procedure involves cutting into an abscess ↓ Likely splash of pus and blood ↓ Infection status unknown ↓ Standard precautions apply to everyone ↓ Choose PPE according to anticipated exposure
exam_trap: A, Waiting for the culture result — it seems logical to tailor protection to the organism, but standard precautions are based on the task and must be in place before any results exist.
takeaway: Choose PPE by assessing the expected exposure from the task, not by the patient's appearance or test results.

stem:
A 26-year-old newly qualified midwife sustains a deep needlestick while suturing a perineal tear. The woman she was caring for is known to be hepatitis B surface antigen positive. The midwife washes the wound but cannot remember whether she completed her hepatitis B vaccine course.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange hepatitis B serology in six weeks and treat if it is positive
options.B: Start a course of oral antibiotics to prevent wound infection
options.C: Begin HIV post-exposure prophylaxis without further assessment
options.D: Book routine occupational health follow-up in three months
options.E: Urgent same-day assessment for hepatitis B prophylaxis

correct_answer: E. Urgent same-day assessment for hepatitis B prophylaxis
why_correct: Significant percutaneous exposure to blood from a hepatitis B surface antigen positive source needs urgent assessment of the worker's vaccination history and antibody response. Depending on this she will need a hepatitis B vaccine dose or an accelerated course, with hepatitis B immunoglobulin in high-risk situations such as being unvaccinated or a known non-responder. Vaccine should be started as soon as possible, and any immunoglobulin given at the same time or within 24 hours and never more than seven days after the exposure, so delay loses protection. Source: UKHSA Green Book chapter 18, Hepatitis B, updated 2026.
why_wrong: A. Waiting to see if she becomes infected misses the window for prophylaxis. B. Antibiotics have no effect on hepatitis B. C. The known risk is hepatitis B, and any HIV prophylaxis still needs formal assessment. D. Routine follow-up is too late for effective prophylaxis.
pearl: A healthcare worker who is a known responder to hepatitis B vaccine usually needs only a booster after exposure, whereas a non-responder needs hepatitis B immunoglobulin.
thinking: Deep needlestick ↓ Source positive for hepatitis B ↓ Her vaccine status is uncertain ↓ Prophylaxis is time-critical ↓ Urgent occupational health assessment
exam_trap: A, Testing serology in six weeks — it seems a measured response, but by then the opportunity for vaccine and immunoglobulin to prevent infection has passed.
takeaway: After exposure to hepatitis B positive blood, seek urgent assessment of immunity and the need for vaccine or immunoglobulin.

stem:
On a haematology day unit, a nurse and an FY1 doctor perform the final bedside check for a unit of red cells for a 58-year-old man with myelodysplasia. The date of birth on his wristband differs by one digit from that printed on the compatibility label, although his name and hospital number agree. He is comfortable and his haemoglobin is stable.

What should happen next?

options.A: Do not transfuse until the laboratory has resolved the mismatch
options.B: Proceed because the name and hospital number both match
options.C: Ask the patient to confirm his birthday verbally and then proceed
options.D: Correct the wristband by hand so that it matches the label
options.E: Start the transfusion slowly with close observation for a reaction

correct_answer: A. Do not transfuse until the laboratory has resolved the mismatch
why_correct: Every identifier on the patient, the prescription and the blood component label must match exactly at the bedside check. Any discrepancy, however minor it seems, means the unit must not be given until the cause is found with the transfusion laboratory. He is stable, so there is no clinical need to take a risk. Source: Guideline on the administration of blood components, British Society for Haematology, 2017.
why_wrong: B. Partial matching is not acceptable; a single mismatch may indicate a wrong-patient sample or label. C. Verbal confirmation does not explain why the documented identifiers differ. D. Altering identification to fit the blood hides the error rather than resolving it. E. Slow infusion does not prevent an ABO-incompatible reaction, which can be fatal after small volumes.
pearl: Wrong blood in tube and bedside checking failures remain among the most frequently reported transfusion errors to SHOT, and ABO incompatibility can be fatal.
thinking: Final bedside check before red cells ↓ One identifier does not match ↓ All identifiers must agree exactly ↓ Patient stable, no urgency ↓ Do not transfuse, resolve with the laboratory
exam_trap: B, Proceeding because the name and hospital number match — two matching details feel reassuring, but transfusion safety depends on every identifier agreeing.
takeaway: Never start a blood component when any patient identifier does not match exactly.

stem:
At 19:45, fifteen minutes before her shift ends on a respiratory ward, an FY2 doctor is phoned by biochemistry with a markedly raised potassium on a 76-year-old man taking spironolactone and ramipril. She asks for an urgent ECG and starts treatment straight away, but review of the response, repeat bloods and further management will fall to the night team. The night doctor arrives shortly.

How should she make sure the rest of his care happens?

options.A: Hand it over directly to the night doctor, stating the actions needed
options.B: Write the result in the medical notes so the night team will see it
options.C: Ask the ward clerk to tell the night doctor when they arrive
options.D: Leave it on the electronic results system for the night team to review
options.E: Rely on the laboratory to telephone the night doctor again

correct_answer: A. Hand it over directly to the night doctor, stating the actions needed
why_correct: A critical result needs a named clinician to take responsibility for acting on it. She has rightly started the urgent steps herself, and the outstanding work, such as reviewing the ECG and his response, repeating the potassium and reviewing his medicines, must be handed over directly to the incoming doctor with the result, its significance and what remains to be done, and the handover recorded. Passive methods risk the result being missed while the patient deteriorates. Source: GMC Good medical practice, continuity of care, 2024.
why_wrong: B. Documentation alone does not guarantee anyone reads it in time. C. A non-clinical colleague cannot convey the urgency or answer clinical questions. D. Results waiting on a system may not be reviewed for hours. E. The laboratory has already informed the team and is not responsible for follow-up.
pearl: Closed-loop communication, where the receiver confirms what they have been told and what they will do, reduces errors in handover.
thinking: Critical result phoned through  ↓  Urgent ECG and treatment started at once  ↓  Further actions still outstanding at shift end  ↓  Responsibility must pass to a named clinician  ↓  Direct verbal handover with actions, then document
exam_trap: B, Writing it in the notes — documentation is good practice, but on its own it does not ensure the incoming doctor knows about an urgent result.
takeaway: A critical result that still needs action must be handed over directly to a named colleague with the actions required.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: urgent ECG/treatment for marked hyperkalaemia must not wait for handover

stem:
A specialty registrar in a busy emergency department has noticed over several months that the sepsis alert on the electronic system often fails to trigger for patients transferred from the minor injuries area. Two near misses have occurred. Mentioning it at team huddles has led to no change.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Bring it up again at the next team huddle
options.B: Contact a local newspaper to make the problem public
options.C: Report it as an incident and escalate to the clinical lead
options.D: Wait until there is actual patient harm so the case is stronger
options.E: Accept that IT problems are outside a doctor's responsibility

correct_answer: C. Report it as an incident and escalate to the clinical lead
why_correct: GMC guidance requires doctors to act promptly when patient safety may be compromised, including by faulty systems or equipment. When informal routes have failed, the concern should be escalated through formal channels such as the incident reporting system and the clinical lead or clinical governance team, and further up, including the Freedom to Speak Up guardian, if it is still not addressed. Source: GMC Raising and acting on concerns about patient safety, 2012 (updated 2024).
why_wrong: A. Repeating the same informal approach has already failed to change anything. B. Going to the media first is not appropriate while internal and regulatory routes have not been used. D. Waiting for harm is unacceptable when the risk is already evident. E. Doctors have a duty to raise any concern that puts patients at risk, including system faults.
pearl: If internal escalation fails, concerns can be raised with a prescribed body such as the CQC or the GMC, and disclosures made this way are protected by whistleblowing law.
thinking: Recurring system fault ↓ Risk of serious harm with near misses ↓ Informal approach failed ↓ Duty to act on safety concerns ↓ Escalate formally through incident reporting and clinical leadership
exam_trap: A, Raising it again at the huddle — it feels collegiate and low key, but it repeats an approach that has already proved ineffective.
takeaway: When informal attempts fail, escalate patient-safety concerns through formal organisational channels.

stem:
A hospital pharmacy team reviews an incident in which a 9-year-old boy on a paediatric ward received ten times the intended dose of intravenous morphine. The prescription had been checked by a pharmacist and two nurses before administration. The ward manager asks how the organisation should respond to the incident report.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Suspend the nurse who gave the dose pending disciplinary action
options.B: Introduce a third checker for opioid doses and close the report
options.C: Arrange retraining for the prescriber and take no further action
options.D: Record the error in each staff member's appraisal and close the incident
options.E: Investigate the system and human factors and act to prevent recurrence

correct_answer: E. Investigate the system and human factors and act to prevent recurrence
why_correct: When an error passes several checks, the problem usually lies in the system, for example look-alike preparations, calculation processes, workload or interruptions, rather than in one individual. A learning-focused review under the NHS Patient Safety Incident Response Framework identifies these contributing factors and leads to changes that reduce the chance of recurrence. A just culture also encourages staff to keep reporting. Source: Patient Safety Incident Response Framework, NHS England, 2022.
why_wrong: A. A blame-based response ignores why multiple checks failed and discourages reporting. B. Adding another check without understanding why the existing ones failed may not help. C. Focusing on one person misses the system factors. D. Recording it against individuals closes the incident without any organisational learning.
pearl: Most medication errors arise from several small weaknesses lining up, as described by the Swiss cheese model.
thinking: Serious error despite several checks ↓ Suggests system weakness ↓ Blame discourages reporting ↓ Analyse human factors and processes ↓ Implement changes to prevent recurrence
exam_trap: B, Adding a third checker — it sounds proactive, but without finding out why three checks already failed, another layer may fail in the same way.
takeaway: Respond to safety incidents by investigating system and human factors, not by blaming individuals.

stem:
An FY1 doctor arrives in a four-bed bay of a care of the elderly ward to take a coagulation screen from a 90-year-old woman. Two of the patients in the bay have the same surname, and the woman greets the doctor by name as she was seen earlier that morning. She is alert and orientated.

Which step is most important before the sample is drawn?

options.A: Read out her name from the request form and ask her to confirm it is correct
options.B: Check the name on the board above her bed
options.C: Rely on recognising her from the earlier review
options.D: Ask her to state her name and date of birth, then check wristband and form
options.E: Take the sample first and then confirm her details when labelling the tube

correct_answer: D. Ask her to state her name and date of birth, then check wristband and form
why_correct: Positive patient identification means the patient states their own full name and date of birth where able, and these are checked against the wristband and the request form before the procedure. This is particularly important when patients with similar names are nearby, as wrong blood in tube errors can lead to misdiagnosis and dangerous treatment. Source: Guideline on the administration of blood components, British Society for Haematology, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Patients may agree to a name read out to them, especially if hard of hearing or confused. B. Bed boards are often wrong or out of date after moves. C. Recognition is unreliable, especially when two patients share a surname. E. Identity must be confirmed before sampling, not after.
pearl: Where a patient cannot state their own details, identity should be confirmed from the wristband and a second reliable source, such as a carer or nurse, following local policy.
thinking: Venepuncture planned ↓ Two patients with the same surname ↓ Familiarity and bed signs are unreliable ↓ Patient states name and date of birth ↓ Check against wristband and request before sampling
exam_trap: A, Reading her name out for confirmation — it seems like checking, but patients often agree with what is said to them, so it is not positive identification.
takeaway: Before taking blood, ask the patient to state their name and date of birth and check against the wristband and request.

stem:
In the emergency department, a doctor draws a full blood count, renal profile and group and save from a 34-year-old man with a lower gastrointestinal bleed. The healthcare assistant offers to label the tubes at the nurses' station so that the doctor can see the next patient.

When and how should the tubes be labelled?

options.A: At the nurses' station by the healthcare assistant, using the electronic record
options.B: Before the next patient is seen, using pre-printed labels made up earlier
options.C: At the end of the shift, using the request forms
options.D: By the doctor at the bedside, straight after taking them
options.E: By the laboratory staff once the request forms arrive with the samples

correct_answer: D. By the doctor at the bedside, straight after taking them
why_correct: Samples should be labelled by the person who took them, at the bedside, immediately after collection and before leaving the patient, having positively identified the patient. Labelling away from the patient, or by someone else, is a major cause of wrong blood in tube errors, which are particularly dangerous for group and save samples used for transfusion. Source: Guideline on the administration of blood components, British Society for Haematology, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Labelling away from the patient by someone who did not take the sample breaks the identification chain. B. Pre-labelling tubes risks them being used for the wrong patient. C. Delayed batch labelling makes mix-ups likely. E. The laboratory cannot verify whose blood is in an unlabelled tube and will reject it.
pearl: For a patient with no previous blood group on record, UK guidance requires a second, independently taken group and save sample to confirm the ABO group before non-urgent red cells are given, unless secure electronic identification is in use, as a safeguard against wrong blood in tube errors.
thinking: Several samples taken ↓ Includes a transfusion sample ↓ Offer to label elsewhere ↓ Identification chain must not break ↓ Sampler labels at the bedside immediately
exam_trap: A, Letting the healthcare assistant label at the nurses' station — it seems efficient, but it separates the tubes from the patient and from the person who took them.
takeaway: The person who takes a blood sample should label it at the bedside immediately, before leaving the patient.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl corrected: two-sample rule applies to first-time patients before non-urgent group-specific red cells, not 'before electronic issue'

stem:
While tidying a phlebotomy tray on an acute medical unit, a nurse finds a filled, unlabelled blood bottle. The FY1 doctor thinks it is probably from one of the three patients he bled in that bay about twenty minutes ago, most likely the man in bed 4.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Label it with the details of the man in bed 4
options.B: Follow local policy: discard it, report an incident and repeat the test
options.C: Send it unlabelled with a note giving the probable patient
options.D: Ask the nurse which patient she thinks it came from and label it accordingly
options.E: Label it from the most likely patient's wristband and phone the laboratory to explain

correct_answer: B. Follow local policy: discard it, report an incident and repeat the test
why_correct: A sample cannot be safely assigned to a patient once its link to that patient has been lost, however confident anyone feels. Local policy should be followed, which normally means disposing of the sample, completing an incident report and taking a fresh, correctly identified and labelled sample. Guessing risks wrong results being acted on, including in transfusion. Source: Guideline on the administration of blood components, British Society for Haematology, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Assigning it on probability could attach another patient's results to him. C. Laboratories reject unlabelled samples and a note does not establish identity. D. Another person's guess is no more reliable. E. Labelling from a wristband after the event still relies on a guess.
pearl: Wrong blood in tube errors are reportable incidents, and for a patient with no blood group on record a second, independently taken sample is usually needed to confirm the ABO group before non-urgent red cells are given.
thinking: Unlabelled filled tube ↓ Several possible patients ↓ Identity cannot be proven ↓ Guessing risks harm ↓ Follow policy: discard, report, repeat
exam_trap: E, Labelling from the likely wristband and phoning the lab — telling the laboratory feels transparent, but the sample's origin is still a guess.
takeaway: Never guess the identity of an unlabelled sample; follow local policy and repeat it.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl corrected to the same accurate two-sample rule wording

stem:
A 79-year-old woman in a community hospital had a urinary catheter inserted during an admission for a fractured neck of femur two weeks ago. She is now mobilising with a frame, can use a commode, and her urine output has been stable for days. Nursing staff ask what to do with the catheter.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Remove the catheter now as it is no longer clinically needed
options.B: Leave it in place until her transfer back to her own home
options.C: Change it for a new catheter every few days to reduce infection
options.D: Start prophylactic antibiotics while the catheter remains
options.E: Clamp the catheter and leave it in situ in case retention develops

correct_answer: A. Remove the catheter now as it is no longer clinically needed
why_correct: The risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection rises with every day an indwelling catheter remains. NICE recommends reviewing the need for a catheter regularly and removing it as soon as possible. She is mobile and able to use a commode, so the catheter should be removed now, with monitoring for retention afterwards. Source: NICE CG139 Healthcare-associated infections: prevention and control in primary and community care, 2012 (updated 2017).
why_wrong: B. Keeping it until discharge adds days of infection risk without benefit. C. Routine frequent changes do not reduce infection and cause trauma. D. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended and promote resistance. E. A clamped catheter still carries infection risk and has no purpose here.
pearl: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is almost universal in long-term catheterised patients and should not be treated with antibiotics.
thinking: Catheter placed for acute illness ↓ Patient now mobile and continent with a commode ↓ No ongoing indication ↓ Infection risk rises with duration ↓ Remove it now
exam_trap: B, Keeping it until discharge — it seems convenient, but every extra day increases the risk of infection.
takeaway: Remove urinary catheters as soon as they are no longer clinically needed.

stem:
A 64-year-old man with dysphagia after a stroke has a fine-bore nasogastric tube placed by a trained nurse on the stroke unit so that enteral feeding can begin. The insertion was straightforward and he is not coughing. The dietitian's feed is ready to start.

What must be done before any feed is given?

options.A: Push air down the tube and listen over the epigastrium for a whoosh
options.B: Place the tube end in water and look for bubbles
options.C: Test the aspirate with litmus paper for an acid reaction
options.D: Test aspirate pH, using a chest X-ray if this cannot confirm position
options.E: Start feeding because an uneventful insertion confirms correct placement

correct_answer: D. Test aspirate pH, using a chest X-ray if this cannot confirm position
why_correct: Feeding through a misplaced nasogastric tube into the lungs is a recognised NHS Never Event. Position must be confirmed before first use by testing aspirate with CE-marked pH indicator paper, with a value of 5.5 or below acceptable. If no aspirate can be obtained or the pH is too high, a chest X-ray interpreted by a competent person is required. Source: NHS Improvement Patient Safety Alert, nasogastric tube misplacement, 2016.
why_wrong: A. The whoosh test is unreliable and must not be used. B. Bubbling in water is unreliable and is not an accepted check. C. Litmus paper is not sensitive enough to distinguish gastric from respiratory aspirate. E. Tubes can enter the airway without coughing, especially after a stroke.
pearl: Tube position should be rechecked before each feed and medication and after any vomiting, coughing episodes or suspected displacement.
thinking: New nasogastric tube for feeding ↓ Misplacement into the airway can be fatal ↓ Bedside signs and air tests are unreliable ↓ Check aspirate pH with pH paper ↓ Chest X-ray if pH test fails
exam_trap: E, Starting feeding after an easy insertion — a smooth insertion and no cough feel reassuring, but tubes can still sit in the airway, especially with impaired swallow and cough reflexes.
takeaway: Confirm nasogastric tube position with aspirate pH testing, or a chest X-ray if that fails, before the first feed.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with COPD arrives in the emergency department acutely short of breath and drowsy but rousable. The team needs an arterial blood gas to assess for type 2 respiratory failure. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation.

Which approach to the sample is most appropriate?

options.A: Stop all oxygen until the gas result is back
options.B: Identify him, explain, use the radial artery and apply prolonged pressure
options.C: Use the femoral artery first because it is the easiest site
options.D: Ignore the anticoagulant, since arterial sampling carries little bleeding risk
options.E: Take the sample immediately and check his identity when labelling

correct_answer: B. Identify him, explain, use the radial artery and apply prolonged pressure
why_correct: An arterial blood gas is an invasive procedure, so he should be positively identified and the procedure explained, with consent obtained as far as his drowsiness allows or the sample taken in his best interests if he lacks capacity. Apixaban is not a contraindication but increases bleeding risk, so a compressible site such as the radial artery is used, with firm, prolonged pressure afterwards. Oxygen should continue, and the result is interpreted alongside his inspired oxygen and clinical state. Source: BTS guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings, British Thoracic Society, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Oxygen should not be withheld from a hypoxic patient; target saturations of 88 to 92 percent are used in COPD. C. The radial artery is the usual first choice; the femoral site has higher risks and is less compressible. D. Anticoagulation increases the risk of haematoma and needs extra care. E. Identity must be confirmed before sampling.
pearl: Record the inspired oxygen concentration with every arterial blood gas, as the result cannot be interpreted without it.
thinking: Acute breathlessness with possible hypercapnia ↓ Arterial gas needed ↓ Identify, explain and consent as able ↓ Anticoagulant increases bleeding risk, use compressible radial site ↓ Interpret with oxygen therapy and clinical state
exam_trap: A, Stopping oxygen until the result returns — it may seem to give a cleaner baseline, but withholding oxygen from a hypoxic patient is dangerous.
takeaway: Perform an arterial blood gas safely with identification, explanation, attention to bleeding risk and interpretation in clinical context.

stem:
A GP practice checked whether patients prescribed long-term lithium had serum levels monitored at the intervals set out in their shared-care protocol and found that only about half did. The team then introduced an automated recall alert in the electronic record. The practice manager asks what must happen now for the audit cycle to be complete.

What is the most appropriate answer?

options.A: Repeat the data collection against the same standard
options.B: Write up the initial findings for a journal
options.C: Randomly allocate patients to receive or not receive alerts
options.D: Switch all patients to an alternative mood stabiliser
options.E: Close the project, as the alert has been introduced

correct_answer: A. Repeat the data collection against the same standard
why_correct: An audit cycle is only closed when practice is measured again against the same standard after the change has been made. Re-auditing shows whether the recall alert has actually improved monitoring, and if not, further changes can be tried and measured in turn. Source: Best practice in clinical audit, Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership, 2016 (reviewed 2020).
why_wrong: B. Publication is optional and does not show whether the change worked. C. Random allocation belongs to research trials, not audit. D. Changing treatment is not an audit step and is clinically unjustified. E. Stopping now leaves the effect of the change unknown, so the loop is never closed.
pearl: The audit loop runs: set standard, measure, compare, implement change, re-measure; it is a cycle that may be repeated many times.
thinking: Standard set and practice measured ↓ Shortfall found ↓ Change introduced ↓ Effect of change unknown ↓ Re-audit against the same standard closes the loop
exam_trap: E, Closing the project once the alert is live — it feels like the job is done, but without re-measurement there is no evidence the change improved care.
takeaway: The audit cycle is completed by re-auditing after a change has been implemented.
notes: Reviewer fix: Removed 3-monthly lithium monitoring figure (conflicts with NICE CG185 interval after first year); now 'intervals in shared-care protocol'

stem:
A 42-year-old man sees the practice nurse alone for a blood pressure check. He mentions that his husband checks his phone every evening, keeps his bank card and has stopped him visiting his family. He asks whether this is 'really abuse' since he has never been hit.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Explain this may be abuse, check his safety and offer support
options.B: Reassure him that without physical violence this is not abuse
options.C: Suggest that the couple attend relationship counselling together
options.D: Tell him he must leave the relationship immediately
options.E: Record the conversation and wait to see if injuries appear

correct_answer: A. Explain this may be abuse, check his safety and offer support
why_correct: Domestic abuse includes controlling or coercive behaviour and economic, emotional and psychological abuse, not just physical or sexual violence, as set out in the statutory definition. Isolating someone from family, monitoring their communication and controlling their money are typical features. He should be told this, asked about his safety and offered support and referral to specialist services. Source: Domestic Abuse Act 2021, section 1, and NICE PH50 Domestic violence and abuse, 2014.
why_wrong: B. Physical violence is not required for behaviour to count as domestic abuse. C. Joint counselling is not recommended where abuse is suspected, as it can increase risk. D. Pressuring him to leave immediately ignores his autonomy and may raise risk. E. Waiting for injuries leaves him unsupported.
pearl: Controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship is a criminal offence in England and Wales under the Serious Crime Act 2015.
thinking: Monitoring, financial control and isolation described ↓ No physical violence ↓ Still meets the definition of domestic abuse ↓ Validate and assess safety ↓ Offer support and referral
exam_trap: C, Couples counselling — it sounds constructive, but joint sessions with a possible abuser can be unsafe and are not advised.
takeaway: Coercive control and financial abuse are domestic abuse even without physical violence.

stem:
A 50-year-old woman receives her first invitation for breast screening and phones her GP surgery, unsure whether to go. She asks the nurse if the test is guaranteed to find any cancer.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Tell her that screening has no downsides, so she should certainly attend
options.B: Explain that an abnormal result would mean she definitely has cancer
options.C: Explain that attending is expected of every woman registered with the practice
options.D: Explain benefits and harms, including overdiagnosis, and let her choose
options.E: Describe only the benefits of screening, so as not to put her off attending

correct_answer: D. Explain benefits and harms, including overdiagnosis, and let her choose
why_correct: Screening is offered, not required, and people should be helped to make an informed choice. That means explaining the potential benefit of early detection alongside the limitations, including false-positive results, missed cancers and overdiagnosis of conditions that might never have caused harm. Her decision should then be respected. Source: NHS breast screening: helping you decide, NHS England (gov.uk), updated 2026.
why_wrong: A. All screening carries potential harms. B. An abnormal screening result needs further tests and does not confirm a diagnosis. C. Participation is voluntary and has no bearing on registration. E. Withholding information about harms prevents informed choice.
pearl: Overdiagnosis, detecting a condition that would never have caused symptoms in a person's lifetime, is a key harm of screening and leads to unnecessary treatment.
thinking: Screening invitation ↓ Patient uncertain ↓ No test is perfect ↓ Explain benefits and harms ↓ Support an informed, voluntary choice
exam_trap: E, Describing the benefits only — it may seem kind and may raise uptake, but omitting the harms undermines informed consent.
takeaway: Screening participation should be an informed choice based on both benefits and harms.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with a small, early-stage breast cancer is told by the surgeon that mastectomy and breast-conserving surgery followed by radiotherapy give similar long-term survival. She lives on a remote island with a long journey to the nearest radiotherapy unit and is the main carer for her mother.

When the options are being discussed with her, which consideration should carry most weight in reaching the choice?

options.A: The operation the breast unit performs most frequently
options.B: The procedure the consultant surgeon personally favours
options.C: Her own priorities, values and practical circumstances
options.D: The option that costs the hospital trust least
options.E: The view of her adult son, who has accompanied her

correct_answer: C. Her own priorities, values and practical circumstances
why_correct: When two treatments offer similar outcomes, the right choice depends on what matters to the individual patient. Her travel burden, caring role and her own feelings about the options are exactly the factors that shared decision-making brings into the discussion. The clinician should explain the options and support her to choose in line with her values. Source: NICE NG197 Shared decision making, 2021, and GMC Decision making and consent, 2020.
why_wrong: A. How often a unit performs an operation does not reflect what suits this particular patient. B. The surgeon's personal preference should inform but not replace her own choice between reasonable options. D. Cost to the trust is not a basis for choosing between equally effective treatments for an individual patient. E. A competent adult makes her own decision; a relative's view can be heard only if she wishes.
pearl: NICE NG197 recommends decision aids and the 'teach-back' approach to check that patients have understood the risks and benefits of each option.
thinking: Two reasonable treatments with equivalent survival ↓ No single clinically superior choice ↓ Her geography and caring duties change the practical burden ↓ Values and circumstances decide between equal options ↓ Support her to choose
exam_trap: B, The consultant's preferred procedure — expert opinion feels authoritative, but when options are clinically equivalent the clinician's role is to inform, not to choose for the patient.
takeaway: When treatments are equally effective, the patient's own values and circumstances should determine the choice.

stem:
On the second day after a hip replacement, a 71-year-old woman has a painful, distended bladder and a bladder scan confirms urinary retention. The foundation doctor is preparing to insert a urethral catheter on the ward.

Which approach is essential for this procedure?

options.A: Explain the procedure, obtain her consent and use aseptic technique
options.B: Use a clean non-sterile technique so the procedure is quicker
options.C: Choose a wide-bore catheter to reduce the chance of blockage
options.D: Insert the catheter first and explain it once she is comfortable
options.E: Leave the catheter in place until discharge to avoid repeat retention

correct_answer: A. Explain the procedure, obtain her consent and use aseptic technique
why_correct: Catheterisation is an invasive procedure, so she needs an explanation and valid consent beforehand. NICE advises that all catheterisations by healthcare workers are aseptic procedures, which reduces the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection, one of the commonest healthcare-associated infections. The smallest gauge catheter that drains effectively is usually chosen, and the need for the catheter should be reviewed regularly. Source: NICE CG139 Healthcare-associated infections: prevention and control in primary and community care, 2012 (updated 2017).
why_wrong: B. A non-sterile technique increases the risk of catheter-associated infection. C. The smallest catheter that drains effectively should be used to limit urethral trauma. D. Explaining afterwards means consent was not obtained. E. Catheters should be removed as soon as they are no longer needed, because infection risk rises with duration.
pearl: The risk of catheter-associated bacteriuria rises with every day a catheter stays in, so its continued need should be reviewed daily.
thinking: Clear indication: urinary retention ↓ Invasive procedure needs explanation and consent ↓ Aseptic technique prevents infection ↓ Smallest suitable catheter ↓ Remove as soon as no longer needed
exam_trap: B, A clean non-sterile technique — it is faster on a busy ward, but it raises the risk of catheter-associated urinary infection.
takeaway: Urethral catheterisation needs consent, aseptic technique, the smallest suitable catheter and prompt removal.
